SafeNexus: Discovering and Steering Modality-Universal Safety Neurons in MLLMs

Probe MLPs for safety neurons shared by text, image, and audio, then steer activations or apply targeted calibration to improve cross-modal safety.

Yu Jian

July 31, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

SafeNexus first identifies safety-related neurons for individual modality settings, then studies their shared intersection. Targeted suppression examines whether these modality-universal neurons influence safety across input combinations, connecting their overlap to observable behavior.

The same coordinates support two interventions: an inference-time activation amplifier and a calibrator that selectively fine-tunes them. These are distinct adaptation routes, allowing the study to compare direct activation control with learned changes to the shared safety mechanism.

US-neuronsModality-universal safety subset
AmplifierInference-time activation control
CalibratorSelective learned adaptation

A cross-modal defense needs a mechanism that remains relevant when the source of risk changes modality.

Why this matters

Extending a language model to images, audio, or combined inputs changes how risks enter the computation. A defense that works for one modality may fail to engage when the same harmful intent reaches the model through another interface.

How it works

  1. Localize functionality-related FFN neurons from intermediate activations and importance scores.
  2. Identify modality-bound safety sets and test the functional relevance of their shared intersection.
  3. Compare activation amplification with targeted calibration on safety, utility, and over-refusal measurements.

What the study finds

Masking modality-universal neurons degrades safety across the tested modality combinations more than matched random controls. The paper evaluates an amplifier and a calibrator on several multimodal models and benchmarks, with additional checks on general capabilities, over-refusal, and transfer to video-related settings.

What this means

The study treats cross-modal consistency as a property of an identifiable internal mechanism. That makes it possible to ask whether a failure comes from missing safety knowledge, limited access to a shared mechanism, or a modality-specific route that does not engage it effectively.

The two intervention routes also clarify the cost of control: changing activations and learning parameter updates solve different adaptation problems. Their comparison can inform when a compact shared target is sufficient, and when broader or differently localized alignment is needed.
